title: Beyond Single-View Indexing: Structure-Aware Multi-View Retrieval for Knowledge-Based VQA
claim: Any single retrieval view fails in distinct, view-specific ways, yet the views overlap strongly, so they complement one another.
layout: 3 regions: left pipeline column, right failure-case table, bottom two Venn diagrams
description: The top-left shows a vertical KB-VQA pipeline of four colored boxes joined by arrows: query image and question, coarse-grained retrieval, fine-grained rerank, and MLLM answering. Dashed lines connect the coarse retrieval box to a large rounded panel on the right titled 'Limitations of Single-View Retrieval'. That panel is a table with three columns, Image view, Title view and Summary view, and rows for query image, ground truth, wrong matches and fail reason. It uses real photos: a castle, a butterfly and wild dogs. Retrieved wrong matches are shown in red-labeled rows, with short failure explanations such as similar visual structure. Along the bottom are two three-set Venn diagrams (Title, Summary, Image) with percentages. They show the share of queries missed by all views, 27% in one diagram and 9% in the other, and how the views overlap.
caption: View-specific failure examples and Recall@20 overlap
abstract: Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) relies on retrieval from large-scale knowledge bases, yet this stage is often treated simplistically. Existing methods typically adopt single-view indexing or naive multi-view fusion, leading to systematic coverage gaps. In this work, we demonstrate that different views exhibit strong complementarity in retrieval. Motivated by this observation, we propose SCAR, a Structure-aware Cross-View Retrieval framework that exploits cross-view structural complementarity at inference time without additional training. SCAR enhances retrieval via structure-aware similarity propagation within each view and explicit cross-view redundancy regulation. Experiments on multiple KB-VQA benchmarks demonstrate that SCAR substantially improves retrieval recall, approaches retrieval coverage upper bounds, and consistently boosts end-to-end KB-VQA performance with negligible inference overhead.
